details.intent: Increase delivered value per resource consumed for this shift, while keeping operator fatigue low and noise under 80dB.

flags.question: Should resource_efficiency be maximised first and human-wellbeing constraints treated as guardrails (raw priority order: efficiency → fatigue → noise), or should fatigue and noise be satisfied first with efficiency optimised only inside that feasible region (compiled priority: HumanWellbeing first) — the two orderings produce materially different schedules when the efficiency-maximising solution sits near the fatigue boundary?
flags.resolution: HumanWellbeing is treated as lexicographically dominant: fatigue ≤ 0.4 and noise ≤ 80 dB are satisfied before any resource_efficiency optimisation is attempted, consistent with the compiled priority_order field.

flags.question: Is there a maximum total resource budget per shift (e.g. an energy ceiling in kWh or a raw-material cap in kg) beyond which additional efficiency gains should not be pursued — given that uncapped maximisation can drive energy consumption up ~40 % above baseline when machine speeds are pushed to their limits?
flags.resolution: No explicit resource ceiling is imposed; the optimiser may increase absolute resource consumption provided the fatigue and noise hard constraints remain satisfied.

flags.question: Is the 0.4 fatigue limit a ceiling that must never be crossed at any instant during the shift, or an end-of-shift accumulated value — because a linear model allows peak-intensity task bursts to push instantaneous fatigue above 0.4 mid-shift while the shift-end value still lands at or below the threshold?
flags.resolution: The 0.4 limit is enforced as an end-of-shift accumulated value; instantaneous intra-shift spikes are not separately constrained unless a real-time fatigue sensor feed is available.

flags.question: If reallocating tasks to fewer operators reduces total labour-hours and thereby raises resource_efficiency, is there a minimum crew size per shift that must be maintained regardless of efficiency gains — since the optimiser could legally assign all tasks to a single operator if no staffing floor is specified?
flags.resolution: The minimum operator count is fixed at the current baseline crew size for the shift; the optimiser may reassign tasks across that crew but may not reduce headcount below the baseline.

flags.question: When equipment_selection causes two or more machines to run concurrently and their combined sound pressure at a workstation exceeds 80 dB (co-located sources add roughly 3 dB per doubling), should the constraint be evaluated at the single worst-case operator workstation or as an area-averaged figure — because the distinction changes which equipment combinations are feasible?
flags.resolution: The 80 dB limit is evaluated at the single loudest occupied operator workstation; combined noise from simultaneously active equipment is computed at that worst-case measurement point using logarithmic addition of individual source levels.

l4_llm_attributions.mechanism: The schedule S1 was designed around a baseline demand of 52 UPH. Actual demand has surged to 65 UPH (+25%), meaning the production quota to be fulfilled by deadline is 25% larger than planned. Compounding this, observed throughput (42.1 UPH) is running below even the original demand baseline of 52 UPH, likely because the station was not provisioned for the higher cycle pressure that demand surge induces. The resulting unit deficit accumulates at roughly 22.9 units per hour (65 UPH required minus 42.1 UPH produced), continuously eroding the deadline buffer. The DeadlineGap constraint—which measures whether scheduled output can be completed within the time window—turns negative as this backlog grows faster than capacity can absorb it. Higher demand also implies elevated cycle pressure on equipment, which can cause micro-stoppages and pace reductions that further suppress throughput below expectations.
l4_llm_attributions.action: Escalate immediately to the production supervisor. Authorize an emergency throughput recovery action: increase robot operating speed to rated maximum (verify noise_db and energy_kwh headroom—current readings of 78 dB and 402 kWh leave margin), reassign any available operators to bottleneck stations to reduce manual-assist latency, and re-sequence remaining Phase 2 jobs to prioritize deadline-critical orders. Simultaneously replan the remainder of S1 against the actual 65 UPH demand figure and issue a revised feasibility assessment for the deadline. If recovery is not achievable within the current shift, initiate customer/stakeholder notification protocol.

l3_repair_suggestions.rationale: The fatigue index of 0.6001 (limit 0.40) is driven directly by the human cycle rate. Reducing from 1.15 to 0.85 (~26% reduction) targets the primary causal lever. Assuming approximately proportional scaling, new fatigue index ≈ 0.6001 × (0.85/1.15) ≈ 0.44, which combined with the buffer_time increase below should bring it below the 0.40 threshold. This is the smallest change that meaningfully addresses the binding fatigue constraint.

Robot r2 is operating at maximum speed (1.0), making it the dominant noise source. A reduction to 0.82 (18% cut) removes peak acoustic output. Noise from robotic systems scales approximately with speed^1.5 to speed^2 (mechanical vibration and air displacement), so an 18% speed reduction yields roughly 3–4 dB reduction, directly attacking the 4.9 dB overage. This is the single smallest speed change that plausibly closes the noise gap without redundantly also cutting r1.

Increasing buffer time from 0.85 to 1.05 s provides additional inter-task rest intervals for the human operator, supplementing the cycle-rate reduction in addressing residual fatigue. Buffer time acts as a secondary fatigue lever without altering the robot speeds or human cycle rate multiplier further. The ~24% buffer increase also smooths pipeline micro-surges that cause intermittent noise spikes near the measurement limit.

details.conflict: A 25.0% demand surge has rendered the current production schedule infeasible under active human-centric constraints. Two violations were detected: (1) FatigueIndex reached 0.6001, exceeding the worker safety limit of 0.40 by a margin of 0.2001 — indicating a high risk of cumulative worker fatigue and associated injury or error; (2) Noise exposure reached 84.9 dB, surpassing the occupational health ceiling of 80.0 dB by 4.9 dB — a level that, with sustained exposure, may cause hearing damage per regulatory standards. The CBPA constraint governance layer has blocked schedule execution and is escalating to the production manager for an authorized remediation decision. No production changes will proceed until a remediation option is selected and logged.
options: Option 1 (Recommended): Extend Horizon via Additional Shift or Workforce Expansion
Option 2 (Moderate Risk): Noise Limit Temporary Relaxation with Mandatory PPE Protocol
Option 3 (High Risk, Last Resort): Dual Constraint Temporary Relaxation with Enhanced Monitoring

details.reasoning_rationale: P(feasible)=0% with FatigueIndex at 100% violation probability and Noise at 80% indicates the current policy is fundamentally unable to handle a +25% demand surge. Prior learning shows S2 was rejected twice while S3 was accepted twice in similar situations, strongly suggesting a policy family switch (S2→S3) is the appropriate remedy. The violations are severe and correlated (not isolated), ruling out MICRO parameter tweaks. However, since prior experience confirms S3 resolves this pattern, full MACRO replanning is unnecessary.
details.reasoning_key_insight: Prior experience with identical disturbance profile consistently rejects S2 and accepts S3 — this is a clear policy misalignment signal requiring a MESO policy family switch, not parameter tuning or full replanning.

experience_synthesis.insight: S2 is deterministically incompatible with demand_surge: both attempts rejected it for identical reasons (Fatigue > 0.4, Noise > 80dB), indicating a structural constraint violation rather than a stochastic failure. S3 is consistently accepted and achieves stable throughput near 42 uph with deadline gaps in the 29–33% range. Prioritize S3 immediately when demand_surge is detected; skip S2 evaluation to save planning cycles. However, with only 2 samples, the deadline_gap_pct variance (2.7 pp spread) and absolute gap magnitude (~30%) warrant monitoring — S3 satisfies constraints but may not fully close deadline gaps at higher surge intensities.
